title: Part 2 — The model at three levels
subtitle: Simple (S), Medium (M) and Complex (C, the rewrite): how much mathematics the main text carries
preface: Each row is one piece of the model or its results. S, M and C are three versions of the main text, left to right; in every version the appendix carries the full Complex treatment, so a lower level moves material to the appendix and loses nothing. Cells that two levels share print once. Each column read top to bottom is a complete main text at its level.\par\smallskip{\small\textbf{Simple, sections:} 2 The economy; 2.1 Tasks; 2.2 Machines, land, and prices; 2.3 Workers; 2.4 The owner and support; 2.5 Equilibrium; 3 Replacement; 3.1 Prices at a given margin; 3.2 The task margin; 3.3 Closing the replacement price; 4 Participation and the labor market; 4.1 The outside option: pricing exit; 4.2 Replacement meets participation; 5 Purchasing power and income; 5.1 What an hour's wage buys; 5.2 Factor income while labor remains employed; 6 Distribution: rent taxation and a uniform transfer; A The general economy and proofs (A.1-A.4) (about 12 pages).\par\textbf{Medium, sections:} 2 Description of the economy; 3 Definition of equilibrium; 3.1 Technology; 3.2 The cost system; 3.3 Households; 3.4 Equilibrium; 4 Equilibrium; 4.1 Prices; 4.2 Participation and the labor market; 4.3 Existence and uniqueness; 5 Purchasing power and income; 5.1 What an hour's wage buys; 5.2 Factor income while labor remains employed; 6 Distribution: rent taxation and a uniform transfer; 6.1 The government; 6.2 Sharing rents; A Proofs and the full statement of the model (appendix) (about 16.0 pages).\par\textbf{Complex, sections:} 2 Description of the economy; 3 Definition of equilibrium; 4 Equilibrium; 5 Purchasing power and income; 6 Distribution: rent taxation and a uniform transfer (about 20 pages).}

rows.title: What the main text carries
rows.diff: S covers only the flow benchmark ($\rho=0$, $\delta=1$) in about 12 pages, in prose with no numbered assumptions or definitions and no proofs, and merges C's Sections 2 and 3 while splitting C's Section~4 into Replacement and Participation; M keeps C's sections, durable machines and statements of the results in about 16 pages, with the cost system in scalar form and every proof in Appendix~A; C takes about 20 pages, with five assumptions, the matrix cost system and the proofs of Propositions 1--3 in the text; S and M introduce the government in Section~6, C in Section~3.5.

options.label: Simple
options.tex:
The main text works in the flow benchmark: a machine lasts one period and nobody discounts ($\rho=0$, $\delta=1$), so a machine-hour costs its current inputs, $p_m=ap_m+\lambda w+br$. It states the environment and the equilibrium conditions in prose, with the key equations displayed. It has no numbered assumptions and no formal definition, uses the scalar machine recursion in place of the matrix system, and brings in the government only in Section~6, where it taxes rents.

Its results are Propositions 1--6, numbered as in the original paper, and Corollaries 1--2 (the original's two unnumbered corollaries), stated in words, each with its key equation: the task margin, the replacement closure, participation and the reservation wage, the purchasing-power bounds, vanishing participation, the income identity, the rent tax, and coverage. Existence and uniqueness is one sentence that points to Appendix~A, and the main text has no proofs.

It keeps five sections (2--6), so Sections 7--10 keep their numbers. Much of it is the authors' own text from the original paper, which mostly works in the flow benchmark. About 12 pages at the paper's density (the original's Sections 3--7, mostly in the flow benchmark, ran 11), against about 20 for Complex. Appendix~A carries everything else in Complex Sections 2--6 (row M.32).

options.label: Medium
options.tex:
\textbf{Medium: Sections 2--6 in about 16 pages} (Complex: 20), typeset at the paper's density. Everything Complex's Sections 2--6 say stays in the paper; the formal apparatus moves to Appendix A, and the economic discussion stays in the main text.
\begin{itemize}
\item The same economy: durable machines ($\delta\in(0,1]$, $\rho\ge0$), a wall $H$ of closed tasks, one non-produced input. Machine-hours rent at the user cost $p_m=(\rho+\delta)V_m$, stated as the condition of a competitive rental market; the owner's problem behind it (Lemma A.1) is in Appendix A.
\item Three numbered assumptions (technology; workers; the owner and support) and one compact Definition 1 for the economy without policy. The assignment is written as a threshold from the start.
\item The cost system in scalar form: the machine recursion as a series, its solution (3), and the price coefficients of each good (4). The matrix system goes to Appendix A.
\item No notation table in the main text; Table 1 becomes Table A.1.
\item Lemma 1, Propositions 1--6, Theorem 1 and Corollaries 1--3 keep their numbers and Complex's statements, with three changes: Proposition 3 and Theorem 1 are stated for the economy without policy, Corollary 2 without its condition on public payments (Section 6.1 adds it), and Corollary 1(i) without its rate (Appendix A). Each is followed by a one-line idea of its proof, and every proof is in Appendix A. The ceiling $x_c$ is defined in prose; Lemma 2 becomes Lemma A.2. The margin-indexed functions are written with Lemma 1's coefficients, (13)--(14).
\item The government enters in Section 6.1, where its instruments are used: its six instruments, the budgets with policy, how Definition 1 extends, and the condition $g_w\le g_e$ of Corollary 2.
\item The remarks on what each result does not depend on move to Appendix A, beside the proofs. The sentences in them that carry economics stay in the text: the closure in any production network, the human-chain bounds (17), recursive automation alone cannot drive $w/r$ to zero, and the case of a wall below the crossing.
\item Unchanged from Complex: Section 2, and the paragraphs on wage premia (M.11), automation in practice and AI (M.13), the loom (M.16), support and enclosure (M.19), and the opening of Section 5 (M.25).
\end{itemize}

options.label: Medium
options.tex:
\optsec{3}{Definition of equilibrium}
The economy described in the preceding section is specified by the relative-productivity schedule $\gamma$ and its wall $x_H$; the recipe $(a,\lambda,b)$ for building a machine and the machine's depreciation rate $\delta$; the land $T$; the number of workers $N$, the space $h$ in a basket, and the distribution $F$ of the costs of work; and the owner's discount factor $\beta$ and utility $u$. We write $\rho=1/\beta-1$ for the owner's rate of time preference, which is the return at which machines are held. The government and its policy enter in Section 6. Table A.1 in Appendix A collects the notation.

rows.title: Tasks
rows.diff: S states the restrictions on the schedule in prose, with the original's sentence that relative human productivity is unbounded at tasks machines cannot perform; M keeps C's prose and states the restrictions as part~(a) of one technology assumption (row M.5); C states them as Assumption~1 (tasks).

options.label: Simple
options.tex:
\optsec{2.1}{Tasks}
Producing one unit of the final good requires a continuum of tasks
$x \in [0,1]$, each in equal amount (Leontief aggregation over tasks): the good's
unit cost is the sum of its tasks' unit costs. One human-hour completes
$\gamma_L(x)$ units of task $x$; one machine-hour completes $\gamma_M(x)$.
Relative human productivity is
\optdisp{\gamma(x) = \gamma_L(x) / \gamma_M(x).}{(1)}
We measure each task in the units an hour completes, $\gamma_L=1$, so that $\gamma(x)$ is the number of machine-hours that do the work of one hour at task $x$.

Some tasks cannot be performed by machines at any price: $\gamma_M(x)=0$ there, so relative human productivity is unbounded. Others are reserved for people, by law or because the good is defined by its human performance. Let $H$ denote the set of tasks closed to machines. We relabel the open tasks so that $\gamma$ increases, assume that $\gamma$ is positive, continuously differentiable and strictly increasing on them, and place the tasks in $H$ after them. The open tasks are then an interval $[0,x_H]$, with $x_H>0$, and $H=(x_H,1]$, which is empty when $x_H=1$. Figure~1 draws $H$ as a wall at the right edge of the schedule. A reservation is a rule: lifting it opens tasks without any change in machines. The schedule $\gamma$ and the set $H$ are given; we do not model the creation of new tasks in which people hold a comparative advantage.

options.label: Medium
options.tex:
\optsec{3.1}{Technology}
The economy has four produced goods (a final good made by performing tasks; machines; the machine-hours that machines supply; and space) and one non-produced input, land.

\textbf{Tasks.} Producing one unit of the final good requires a continuum of tasks
$x \in [0,1]$, each in equal amount (Leontief aggregation over tasks): the good's
unit cost is the sum of its tasks' unit costs. One human-hour completes
$\gamma_L(x)$ units of task $x$; one machine-hour completes $\gamma_M(x)$.
Relative human productivity is
\optdisp{\gamma(x) = \gamma_L(x) / \gamma_M(x).}{(1)}
It is the number of machine-hours that do the work of one hour at task $x$. Some tasks are closed to machines: machines cannot perform them, $\gamma_M(x)=0$, or they are reserved for people, by law or because the good is defined by its human performance. We relabel the open tasks so that $\gamma$ increases, which changes the measure of no set of tasks, and we place the closed tasks after them; Figure 1 draws the closed tasks as a wall at the right edge of the schedule. A reservation is a rule: lifting it opens tasks without any change in machines. The schedule $\gamma$ and the set of closed tasks are exogenous; new versions of tasks in which people hold a comparative advantage would raise $\gamma$ at the tasks they replace, the reverse of task automation (Section 3.4), and we do not model their creation.

options.label: Medium
options.tex:
\textbf{Machines and land.} A machine is itself produced: from other machines, from labor, and from land, such as a site, a mineral deposit, or the ground under a plant or a datacenter. Land services are used to build machines and, rented directly, as living space: a unit of space is a unit of land services.

\begin{optthm}{Assumption 1}{technology}
(a) \emph{Tasks.} One hour completes one unit of every task, $\gamma_L=1$. The tasks closed to machines form the set $H=(x_H,1]$, with $x_H\in(0,1]$, so that $H$ is empty when $x_H=1$. On the open tasks $[0,x_H]$, $\gamma$ is positive and continuously differentiable, with $\gamma'(x)>0$ for $0<x<x_H$.
(b) \emph{Machines.} Building a machine takes $a\ge0$ machine-hours, $\lambda\ge0$ hours of labor, and $b>0$ units of land services. A machine supplies one machine-hour per period, and a fraction $\delta\in(0,1]$ of the machine stock wears out each period. Moreover, $(\rho+\delta)(a+\lambda\gamma(0))<1$.
(c) \emph{Land.} There are $T>0$ units of land, each yielding one unit of land services per period. No activity adds to the land.
\end{optthm}

Part (a) restricts only the relabeled schedule, which has no jumps or flat stretches below $x_H$. The last condition in (b) has two parts: $(\rho+\delta)a<1$, so that machine-hours have a finite price, and, at the first task, the machine-hours that replace an hour of work cost less than that hour at a high enough wage (Section 4.3). With $\rho=0$ and $\delta=1$ a machine lasts one period and earns no return, so machine services are priced at their current cost; we call this case the flow benchmark. We write $r$ for the rent on land services; it is not an interest rate.

rows.title: Margins and automation
rows.diff: S defines the margins and the two automation channels in prose, keeping the original's paragraph on the channels whole, which brings here the two loom sentences that C has in row M.13 and the software-developer example that C drops; M states Definition~2 directly on the threshold and keeps C's Definition~3; C states Definition~2 on sets of tasks of positive measure and then reads it on the threshold.

options.label: Simple
options.tex:
The margin is \emph{interior} when $0<x^*<x_H$, so that machines perform a set of tasks of positive measure and labor performs a set of open tasks of positive measure. The assignment is a \emph{boundary assignment} when $x^*=x_H$, so that labor holds almost none of the open tasks, and a \emph{corner} when $x^*=0$. At a boundary assignment there is no open marginal task, and the machine comparison does not pin the wage. An interior margin can coexist with human-required tasks in $H$. Appendix~E treats the case in which human-required services determine the wage.

\textbf{Task automation} improves machine capability at tasks near the assignment margin, lowering relative human productivity there. A faster loom reduces the machine time needed to replace an hour of weaving. \textbf{Recursive automation} reduces the human hours embodied in machine services, $\widetilde{\lambda}_m$. Automating the manufacture and maintenance of looms can lower the labor required to supply a loom-hour. Software developers illustrate how the two channels can meet: generating code automatically changes the machine alternative to a programming task; when that work builds or maintains systems supplying machine services, fewer developer hours can also reduce the labor embodied in those services.

In this economy, task automation lowers $\gamma$ at some tasks and can move tasks out of $H$ that were closed to machines by capability. Recursive automation lowers $\lambda$, the labor needed to build a machine, and with it $\widetilde\lambda_m=\lambda/(1-a)$.

options.label: Medium
options.tex:
Labor, at wage $w$, holds task $x$ when it is the cheaper input:
$w/\gamma_L(x) \le p_m/\gamma_M(x)$, i.e.
$w \le p_m\cdot\gamma(x)$. The right-hand side is labor's \emph{replacement value} at task $x$: the wage at which labor and the machine alternative cost the same there. Figure 1 draws the schedule.

\begin{optthm}{Proposition 1}{the task margin}
In an equilibrium with $w>0$ and $p_m>0$:
(i) at an interior margin,
\optdisp{w=p_m\gamma(x^*);}{(8)}
at a boundary assignment, $w\ge p_m\gamma(x_H)$; at a corner, $w\le p_m\gamma(0)$.
(ii) Holding the machine rental fixed, movement of an interior margin changes the wage at rate $dw/dx^*=p_m\gamma'(x^*)$. Where a fixed-output labor-demand schedule absorbs additional final-task hours by lowering $x^*$, a steeper capability schedule requires a larger wage change for the same movement of the margin.
\end{optthm}
Part (i) follows from condition (i) of Definition 1 and the continuity of $\gamma$; part (ii) differentiates (8) at a fixed rental (Appendix A).

rows.title: The ceiling (Lemma 2)
rows.diff: S and M define the ceiling in prose, S in its flow form $a+\lambda\gamma(x)\ge1$ and M with $\rho$ and $\delta$, and state the lemma in Appendix~A as Lemma~A.2; C states it as Lemma~2 with a remark; all three explain why machines cannot undercut labor at the ceiling or beyond it.

options.label: Simple
options.tex: In every equilibrium, machines perform almost none of the open tasks at or above the \emph{ceiling} $x_c$, the first open task at which $a+\lambda\gamma(x)\ge1$, or $x_H$ if there is none. At such a task the machine-hours that would replace an hour embody at least that hour of labor, $\gamma(x)\widetilde\lambda_m\ge1$, counting the labor needed to build them, so they cost at least the hour at any wage. Since $a+\lambda\gamma(0)<1$, the ceiling lies above the first task. Unlike $H$, the ceiling depends on the labor in the machine chain as well as on capability.

options.label: Medium
options.tex:
\optsec{4.3}{Existence and uniqueness}
Let $x_c$ be the first open task at which $(\rho+\delta)(a+\lambda\gamma(x))\ge1$, or $x_c=x_H$ if there is none; we call it the ceiling, and Assumption 1(b) gives $x_c>0$. At a task in $[x_c,x_H]$, the machine-hours that would replace an hour embody at least that hour of labor, counting the labor needed to build them at the required return, so they cost at least the hour at any wage. In every equilibrium, therefore, machines perform almost no task from $x_c$ on (Lemma A.2). Unlike $H$, the ceiling depends on the labor in the machine chain and on the return, as well as on capability.

rows.title: Labor demand and supply along the margin
rows.diff: S writes the wage--rent ratio and labor demand and supply along the margin in one display in flow form; M writes them with Lemma~1's coefficients in two displays; C writes out every price and quantity in four displays with durable machines and ends with the limit of $v/P_s$ at a binding ceiling, which S and M move to Appendix~A with C's closed forms.

options.label: Simple
options.tex:
At an interior margin $x$ below the ceiling, with $r=1$, the closure (11) and the basket's requirements (9) give the wage--rent ratio, the basket's price, and the quantities as functions of the margin. Labor demand and supply are
\optdisp{v(x)=\frac{\gamma(x)\,b}{1-a-\lambda\gamma(x)},\qquad
N_D(x)=Y(x)\left[1-x+\frac{\lambda J(x)}{1-a}\right],\qquad
N_S(x)=NF\left(\log\left[1+\frac{v(x)}{P_s(x)}\right]\right),}{(16)}
where $Y(x)=T/B_s(x)$ and $P_s(x)=v(x)L_s(x)+B_s(x)$, with $L_s(x)$ and $B_s(x)$ given by (9) at $x$. The two components of demand are final-task and machine-sector hours. As $x$ rises to $x_c$, $N_S(x)$ tends to a limit, which we write $N_S(x_c)$.

options.label: Medium
options.tex:
At an interior threshold $x<x_c$, machines perform tasks below $x$ and people those above it. By (8), (9) and Lemma 1(i), with $r=1$, the wage--rent ratio, the machine rental, and the basket's price at that threshold are
\optdisp{v(x)=\gamma(x)\,p_m(x),\qquad
p_m(x)=\frac{(\rho+\delta)b}{1-(\rho+\delta)(a+\lambda\gamma(x))},\qquad
P_s(x)=v(x)\widetilde\lambda_s(x)+\widetilde b_s(x),}{(13)}
where $\widetilde\lambda_s(x)$ and $\widetilde b_s(x)$, like $L_s(x)$ and $B_s(x)$ below, are the coefficients of Lemma 1 with $x$ in place of $x^*$. With all land in use, Lemma 1(ii) gives output $Y(x)=T/B_s(x)$, and labor demand and supply are
\optdisp{N_D(x)=\frac{TL_s(x)}{B_s(x)},\qquad
N_S(x)=NF\left(\log\left[1+\frac{v(x)}{P_s(x)}\right]\right).}{(14)}
The two components of demand are final-task and machine-sector hours. As $x$ rises to $x_c$, $N_S(x)$ tends to a limit, which we write $N_S(x_c)$. The denominator of $p_m(x)$ is positive at every open task below the ceiling.

rows.title: Existence and uniqueness (Theorem 1)

rows.diff: M's text is C's, renumbered, because M has C's durable machines and, from Section~6.1, C's public provision of the basket; S derives the tax rate that funds one basket per person from a uniform transfer equal to the basket's price, as the original did, and leaves the instance's split of support between rent and the return on machines to Appendix~A.3.

options.label: Simple
options.tex:
Rent revenue can finance the basket underlying the participation choice. Define coverage by $\kappa=R/(NP_s)$, with $R>0$. Funding exactly one basket per person requires $d=P_s$, hence
\optdisp{\tau_R=\frac{NP_s}{R}=\frac{1}{\kappa}.}{(21)}
A tax rate between zero and one can meet this budget exactly when $\kappa\ge1$, evaluated at equilibrium prices. Appendix~D.3 relates coverage to the basket's input requirements.

Replacing existing household or public financing while maintaining total support and prices leaves the participation comparison unchanged. If the payment supplements the existing basket, Section~2.3's preferences instead give the reservation wage $(e^\chi-1)(P_s+d)$: the extra consumption available in both states reduces the gain from work. Redistribution can also change demand, rents, and the resources of support providers. These equilibrium effects determine whether the promised basket remains funded.

With no tax, the owner's budget (7) requires $rT\ge NP_s$, so every equilibrium has $\kappa\ge1$. The measured coverage, $0.30$ (Section~8), therefore fits this economy only with another source of support (Appendix~A.3).

A wage-funded transfer draws on the labor market as both a financing base and a participation margin. Its incidence depends on demand and supply elasticities. The limiting case also constrains how much support that base can finance.

options.label: Simple
options.tex:
\textbf{Appendix A. The general economy and proofs.} Appendix~A carries everything in Complex Sections 2--6 that the main text does not, so the main text's results are the flow case ($\rho=0$, $\delta=1$) of the appendix's. Its results are numbered A.1, A.2, and so on; Proposition~A.$k$ is Complex's Proposition~$k$, of which the main text's Proposition~$k$ is the flow case.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{A.1 The economy with durable machines.} Complex Section~3 in full: Table~A.1 (notation); Assumptions A.1--A.5 (tasks, machines, land, workers, the owner), with depreciation $\delta$, the owner's discount factor $\beta$ and utility $u$, and the return $\rho=1/\beta-1$; the user cost $p_m=(\rho+\delta)V_m$ and the price of a machine; the matrix system (3)--(4) with $\mathbf A_\rho$ and $\mathbf A_0$; the workers' Leontief utility and budget with public payments; the owner's sequential budget; the government's six instruments and its budget; Definitions A.1--A.3 (equilibrium, margins, automation), the matrix form of the clearing conditions, and Walras's law.
\item \textbf{A.2 Equilibrium.} Complex Section~4's statements: Lemma~A.1 (prices and quantities, with price coefficients no smaller than the physical requirements); Propositions A.1--A.3 with their remarks (A.2 reading $\gamma(x^*)\widetilde\lambda_m$ on the price basis, A.3 with the instruments at zero); Lemma~A.2 (the ceiling); the margin-indexed prices and quantities (21)--(24) with $\rho$ and $\delta$, and the limit of $v/P_s$ at a binding ceiling; Theorem~A.1 (existence and uniqueness, with funding $rT+\rho V_mX\ge NP_s$) and its remark; Corollary~A.1 (labor supply and the margin) and its remark.
\item \textbf{A.3 Purchasing power, income, and rent taxation with durable machines.} Propositions A.4--A.6 and Corollaries A.2--A.3 as Complex states them, with their remarks: the price-basis reading of $\widetilde b_i$; Corollary~A.2 with public payments ($g_w\le g_e$) and the bound on participation when a payment favors work; Proposition~A.5 with the return on machines, $I=wN_a+rT+\rho V_mX$, labor's share as an inequality, and the instance's split of income (0.55 wages, 0.13 rent, 0.32 return); Proposition~A.6(iii) and Corollary~A.3 with the return beside rent; (16) under public provision; the instance's coverage (rent 0.38 of support); Corollary~A.3(ii) in $\widetilde b_s$, with its remark (such a configuration is not an equilibrium; the condition with several inputs; durable machines, 1.71 and 0.66 baskets per person); and the five statements that durable machines change.
\item \textbf{A.4 Proofs.} The current Appendix~A: the owner's problem (now Lemma~A.3) and its remark, and the proofs of every result in A.2 and A.3, including those of Propositions 1--3 that Complex gives in the text.
\end{itemize}
Appendices B--F are unchanged.

\item Table 1 (notation), as Table A.1.
\item The owner in full: Assumption 5's conditions on $u$ and the long-run criterion at $\beta=1$; the period-by-period budget (10); Lemma A.1 and its remark (the user cost as the owner's first-order condition when $c_o>0$, and why it does not bind at $c_o=0$).
\item The cost system in matrix form: the unit cost (2) for any set $\mathcal M$ of machine tasks; the price system (3) with $\mathbf A_\rho$, $\bm\lambda$, $\mathbf b$; the price coefficients (4); $\mathbf A_0$ and the physical coefficients $(\mathbf I-\mathbf A_0)^{-1}\bm\lambda$, $(\mathbf I-\mathbf A_0)^{-1}\mathbf b$; and the matrix form of the clearing conditions, with $\mathbf y$ and $\mathbf z$.
\item Complex's Definition 1 with the full policy and Definition 2 for a set $\mathcal M$ of machine tasks, with the step from cost minimization to a threshold; Section 3.5's government paragraph; and the workers' budget (8) of Complex.
\item Lemma 2 (the ceiling) and its remark, as Lemma A.2, with its proof; Complex's closed forms (18)--(21) for $p(x)$, $Y(x)$ and $X(x)$.
\item The proofs of Propositions 1--3 (in Complex's main text), including Proposition 2's derivatives and Proposition 1(ii)'s $N_F$; the proofs of Lemma 1, Theorem 1, Corollaries 1--3 and Propositions 4--6, as in Complex's Appendix A.
\item Corollary 2 as Complex states it, with public payments and $g_w\le g_e$, the example of a payment that favors work, and the proofs that Lemma 1 and Propositions 1, 2, 4 and 5 hold with any policy.
\item The remarks on what each result does not depend on, beside each proof; with them Complex's notes that Lemma 1(iii) extends to every good (Proposition B.1(a)), that Corollary 2 holds good by good in a network, that Theorem 1's uniqueness rests on the user-cost clause, and Proposition 6's remark on a tax on rent received.
\item From Complex's text after Definition 1: the user-cost clause when support absorbs all the owner's income, and Walras's law.
\item Corollary 1(i)'s rate $dv/dx$ and its factor $1+\lambda v/b$; the limit of $v/P_s$ at the ceiling.
\item Section 5.2's paragraph on the five statements that need $\rho=0$, and the instance's income shares (0.55, 0.13, 0.32; labor's share 0.55 against the bound 0.81).
\item Corollary 3's remark: why its part (ii) is not an equilibrium, the coverage formula with several inputs and its reading input by input at $\rho=0$, and the durable-machine numbers 1.71 and 0.66.
\end{itemize}
Appendices B--F are unchanged.
